item.title: How this site is built
item.description:
Academic pages are usually a PDF CV and a list of links. This one is a Quarto project: the same toolchain I use for analysis reports, pointed at a website. The practical consequence is that a figure here is never a screenshot — it is code that runs at build time, and if the underlying data changes, the figure changes with the next push.

The stack

Layer Tool Why
Content Quarto .qmd Markdown plus executable R chunks
Analysis R, tidyverse The language the actual work is done in
Interactive figures Plotly, Leaflet, DT Zoom, hover and layers without a server
Client-side interaction Observable JS Sliders that recompute in the browser
Build GitHub Actions Renders on every push to main
Hosting GitHub Pages Static, free, versioned

The part worth copying

execute: freeze: auto in _quarto.yml caches chunk results in _freeze/. Commit that directory and the build runner never has to install R or restore packages: it serves the cached output and renders the HTML. Builds drop from several minutes to a few seconds, and a package update upstream cannot silently change a published figure.

The trade-off is that you re-render locally when data changes, and commit the cache along with the code. For a site whose figures come out of a dissertation pipeline, that is the right direction: the published version should change when I decide it changes, not when CRAN does.

Client-side, not Shiny

Shiny needs a server. Observable JS does not: ojs_define() writes an R object into the page as JSON, and the browser does the rest. Every interactive control on the Research page works from a static file, which is why the whole site fits on GitHub Pages at no cost.
